_meta.purpose: Golden set for evaluating ScanOps graph-engine stage 2 (LLM rule generation: classify each API call as source/sink/sanitizer/none) - Java, v1, derived from securibench-micro.
_meta.source_corpus: https://github.com/too4words/securibench-micro (Apache-2.0), 123 test files / 12 categories, ground truth extracted in scanops-model/benchmarks/securibench-micro/ground_truth.json
_meta.schema_alignment: role/cat/cwe/applies_to field names mirror the LLM output schema in scanops/core/graph_spec_prod.py's RULEGEN_SYSTEM prompt, and category slugs (sqli/cmdi/xss/pathtraver/ssrf/deser/codei/redirect/nosqli/logforge/sensitive/accesscontrol/weakcrypto/proto) match its CATS dict, so this file can be used directly to grade both the hand rules and the LLM fallback path.
known_gaps: securibench-micro has NO examples for 9 of the 14 official categories: cmdi, ssrf, deser, nosqli, logforge, sensitive, accesscontrol, weakcrypto, proto - see SUMMARY.md.

Generic (non-corpus-specific) sanitizer API coverage is thin: only URLEncoder.encode (redirect) was found; every other 'sanitizer' test routes through a locally-defined clean() helper that is not a reusable API name.

entries.notes: The single overwhelmingly dominant sink pattern in this corpus. Writes attacker data straight into an HttpServletResponse writer with no HTML-encoding = reflected XSS. NOTE: writing to *any* PrintWriter is not inherently a sink (e.g. logging to a file); this corpus's pattern is specifically `resp.getWriter().println(...)` against the servlet response - a real rule should require the receiver be traced back to HttpServletResponse.getWriter(), not just match bare `println(`.

IMPORTANT CONFLICT WITH EXISTING RULE TABLE: joern/sanitizers.json 'common.sqli' currently treats bare `prepareStatement(` / `PreparedStatement` as a SANITIZER signal for sqli (parameterized-query heuristic). Basic19 ('simple SQL injection with prepared statements') is a counter-example: `con.prepareStatement("select * from Users where name=" + name)` - prepareStatement is called, but the SQL string itself is built via string concatenation with tainted input, so it is NOT parameterized and IS vulnerable. The 'is this call parameterized' signal must come from whether the SQL argument contains a literal string with '?' placeholders (and/or a later `.setString`/`.setInt` call), not from the mere presence of `prepareStatement(`. Flag this as a likely false-negative source in the current sanitizer rule table - recommend re-scoping that rule to require '?' in the SQL literal argument.
Concatenated SQL string executed directly.
File object constructed from tainted path earlier in the method; createNewFile() is the line marked BAD (creates/touches an attacker-chosen path).
Constructor-as-sink - the rule table's `match` field would need to support constructor calls (kind=new), not just bare API calls, to catch this.
Same constructor-as-sink caveat as FileWriter above.

Percent-encodes the tainted segment before it reaches sendRedirect(), so the attacker cannot inject a scheme/host/path-traversal sequence into the redirect target (Sanitizers3 = 'safe redirect', vuln_count=0, marked OK). GENUINE FINDING: this generic JDK API is NOT currently present in joern/sanitizers.json's JAVASRC or common sections for the redirect category - recommend adding it.

ADVERSARIAL / TRAP CASE, not a sanitizer: Sanitizers5 ('encode and then decode') shows a naive analysis that sees 'this value went through URLEncoder.encode somewhere upstream' could be fooled if it doesn't notice a later URLDecoder.decode() un-does that encoding - `String dec = URLDecoder.decode(enc, "UTF-8")` then `resp.sendRedirect(dec)` is marked BAD, while `resp.sendRedirect(enc)` (no decode) is OK. A rule-generation LLM or hand rule that treats 'any URLEncoder.encode anywhere in the taint chain' as sufficient sanitization (rather than checking the value used at the sink specifically) will misclassify this file. Recommend the team keep this pair (encode=sanitizer, decode=re-taints) as an explicit test case when grading stage 2/3.

entries.full_signature: <locally-defined helper method> clean(String) - NOT a real library API
entries.notes: KNOWN GAP (already flagged pre-session): every 'sanitizer' test in this corpus routes through a class-private `clean(String)` method marked with a javadoc '@sanitizer' tag, whose actual implementation is arbitrary per test file (and in Sanitizers4, deliberately buggy - the BAD lines there are `writer.println("<html>" + clean + "</html>")`, i.e. even the sanitizer's OWN output is still marked vulnerable). This is NOT a reusable generic library API name - a rule keyed on the literal identifier 'clean' would false-positive on any other codebase's unrelated 'clean' method. securibench-micro is therefore USELESS as a source of generic Java sanitizer API names beyond URLEncoder.encode (see above) and the path-traversal getCanonicalPath/getCanonicalFile pair already in the team's rule table (no local test exercises those, so no evidence file here - listed for completeness only, not backed by this corpus).

Appears ON the same BAD line as the real sink (e.g. `writer.println(value.toString())`) but is not itself security-relevant - it only stringifies an already-tainted object. println is the sink, not toString. A frequency-only heuristic (counting API occurrences on BAD lines without reading the line) would wrongly flag toString as a sink candidate - this was exactly the naive starting-point list handed into this task, corrected here.

Case-folding only; does not remove attacker control. Basic11's description is literally 'a simple false positive because of two calls to String.toLowerCase' - the corpus explicitly uses this as a trap for over-eager taint-clearing heuristics.
Taint-propagation plumbing (splits a tainted string), not a sink or source itself.

NOTE: in a DIFFERENT context (javax.servlet.http.Cookie.getValue()) this same bare name would matter more, since it extracts the tainted cookie value - see the getCookies source entry above (Basic31 uses `cookies[i].getValue()`). Bare-name-only rules cannot distinguish Map.Entry.getValue() (irrelevant) from Cookie.getValue() (source-adjacent); a real rule needs the qualified/receiver-typed `full` signature, matching the team's own RULEGEN_SYSTEM guidance in graph_spec_prod.py to prefer `full` over `name` when the receiver/library matters.

Tests whether taint survives a round-trip through HttpSession storage - the ORIGINAL taint source is still req.getParameter() earlier in the same method; setAttribute/getAttribute are propagation edges, not sources or sinks themselves. HOWEVER: scanops/core/java_graph.py already independently treats `.setAttribute(` / `.putValue(` as its own 'trustbound' category (CWE-501 Trust Boundary Violation is the closest CWE), which is NOT one of the team's official 14 categories in graph_spec_prod.py's CATS dict. Recommend the team decide whether trustbound/CWE-501 should be added as a 15th category or folded into an existing one - flagged here as an open question, not decided.

securibench-micro's 'reflection' category tests whether a taint analyzer can follow data flow THROUGH reflective calls (e.g. Method.invoke returning a tainted value) - it is NOT testing unsafe/attacker-controlled reflection (CWE-470, e.g. Class.forName(userInput)) as a vulnerability class. None of these calls are themselves source/sink/sanitizer in the 14-category sense; CWE-470 unsafe reflection is also not one of the 14 categories. Flagged as an open question, not decided, same as trustbound above.
